To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the binding energy is a sum of several components and the relative importance of each of them depends on the nature of the binding process.

the binding free energy is the sum of the solvation free energy and the internal free energy, that the solvation free energies can be decomposed into electrostatic and non-electrostatic contributions, that the electrostatic solvation free energy is the difference between the electrostatic free energies of the complex and the unbound molecules, that the electro-static free energies of the molecules are calculated by the linear response approximation, that the non-electrostatic solvation free energies are calculated by a linear response model,

the energy components governing the binding phenomena can be grouped into four categories, i.e. electrostatics, van der Waals, solvation and conformational energy, that the continuum approaches are quite successful in predicting the binding affinity, provided that the energy components are described in a proper way, and that a rigorous approach to predict the binding affinity should consider all energy components on the same footing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the energy components of the binding process and the ways in which the knowledge of these components can be used to improve the accuracy of the continuum approaches.
the development of methods for predicting binding affinity of small molecules to proteins and other biomacromolecules.
the development of a rigorous continuum approach to the calculation of binding affinity and the identification of the energy components governing the binding free energy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a proper description of the energy components of binding affinity, in the continuum context, is a key issue in the field.

the continuum approaches are very powerful tools to predict the binding affinity and the knowledge of the individual energy contributions could help to understand the molecular recognition process in detail.
the continuum approaches are a very useful tool in predicting binding free energy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding free energy is not a simple sum of the individual energy contributions but a complex interplay of the various energy terms.
the binding free energy can be described as a combination of the electrostatic, van der Waals and polarizability components.

the binding free energy is a sum of the individual energy components and the binding affinity can be predicted by either using the sum of the components or by utilizing the individual components to construct a binding free energy equation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the continuum framework is capable to capture the major energy contributions governing molecular recognition, provided the proper description of the physical processes taking place during the binding.
the binding free energy can be decomposed into a number of components, which are related to specific interactions and physical processes taking place in the binding site.
continuum approaches can be further improved by incorporating the atomistic details into their formulation.
